subject: political-science
readings: OD ch. 6 (Orvis & Drogus, *Institutions of Participation and Representation*)

cards.front: What is Pitkin's **formalistic** representation?
cards.back: The institutional arrangement that **authorises** a representative and holds them **accountable**. Elections are the "before" and "after".

cards.front: What is Pitkin's **descriptive** representation?
cards.back: The representative **resembles** the represented (gender, ethnicity, class): "standing for". It is the main argument for **quotas**.
cards.hint: Looks like the people it serves.

cards.front: What is Pitkin's **symbolic** representation?
cards.back: The representative **stands for** the represented symbolically, like a leader or flag that people identify with.
cards.hint: A leader or flag people identify with.

cards.front: What is Pitkin's **substantive** representation?
cards.back: The representative **acts in the interests** of the represented: "acting for".

cards.front: Who distinguished four senses of representation (formalistic, descriptive, symbolic, substantive)?
cards.back: **Hanna Pitkin**, in *The Concept of Representation* (1967).

cards.front: Which of Pitkin's senses is a legislature that **looks like** the population it serves?
cards.back: **Descriptive** representation ("standing for"), the argument for quotas.

cards.front: Which of Pitkin's senses is a monarch or flag that people **identify with**?
cards.back: **Symbolic** representation.

cards.front: Which of Pitkin's senses is elections that **authorise and hold a representative accountable**?
cards.back: **Formalistic** representation.

cards.front: Which of Pitkin's senses is an MP who **acts in your interests**?
cards.back: **Substantive** representation ("acting for").

cards.front: Within substantive representation, contrast the **delegate** and **trustee** models.
cards.back: 1) **Delegate:** follows instructions, mirroring constituents' expressed wishes. 2) **Trustee:** uses their own judgment of the constituents' best interests. Both are "acting for".
cards.hint: Follow the mandate vs use your own judgment.

cards.front: Which Pitkin sense does **PR** most boost, and which does **SMD** emphasise?
cards.back: **PR** boosts **descriptive** representation (lists and quotas seat more women and minorities). **SMD** emphasises the **formalistic** local link (one district representative you can vote out).
cards.hint: Lists and quotas vs one local name.

cards.front: Who argued that for most people voting is technically **irrational**?
cards.back: **Downs** (1957). One vote almost never decides the outcome.
cards.hint: 1957; the seed of the collective action problem.

cards.front: Why is participation a **collective action problem**?
cards.back: Individuals rationally choose not to vote, yet all suffer if nobody does.

cards.front: If voting is individually irrational, why do people vote anyway?
cards.back: 1) **Expressive and solidaristic** reasons. 2) Charismatic leaders. 3) To avoid the **emotional cost** of not voting (guilt, exclusion).

cards.front: How do institutions shape voter turnout?
cards.back: 1) Complex systems depress turnout among the less educated. 2) **PR and mixed systems raise it** (fewer wasted votes). 3) Parties and interest groups lower the cost of finding and acting on your interests.
cards.hint: Complexity down, PR up, parties lower cost.

cards.front: Name the four families in the electoral system menu.
cards.back: 1) **SMD plurality (first past the post)**. 2) **Majoritarian**. 3) **Proportional representation (PR)**. 4) **Mixed / semiproportional**.

cards.front: Which electoral system: most votes in each single member district wins, no majority needed?
cards.back: **SMD plurality**, also called **first past the post**.

cards.front: What are the strengths and weaknesses of **first past the post**?
cards.back: **Strengths:** strong voter representative link, single party government, clear accountability. **Weaknesses:** **wasted votes**, **disproportionality** (a party can win big on ~35% pluralities), gerrymandering, fewer women and minorities.

cards.front: What is **gerrymandering**?
cards.back: Drawing single member district boundaries to rig outcomes, packing and cracking opponents into losing configurations.

cards.front: The term "gerrymander" combines which governor's name with what animal shape?
cards.back: Governor **Elbridge Gerry** plus a **salamander** shaped Massachusetts district (1812).

cards.front: Which electoral family requires the winner to clear an absolute majority (50%+1)?
cards.back: **Majoritarian** systems (the two round runoff or the Alternative Vote).

cards.front: Walk through an **Alternative Vote** count with A 40%, B 35%, C 25%.
cards.back: Voters **rank** candidates 1, 2, 3. Count first preferences; nobody has 50%. **Eliminate last placed C** and transfer C's ballots to next choices (say +18%→B, +7%→A). New totals: A 47%, B 53% → **B wins**, though A led the first count.

cards.front: Contrast the **two round system** and the **Alternative Vote**.
cards.back: Both need 50%+1. 1) **Two round (France):** if no majority, top candidates meet in a **second election** a week or two later. 2) **Alternative Vote:** one ballot, rank candidates, eliminate the last and transfer **instantly** until one passes 50%.
cards.hint: Two separate elections vs one instant runoff.

cards.front: What did **Maine 2018** demonstrate about ranked choice voting?
cards.back: The first US Congress seat decided by the Alternative Vote: Golden won **50.5 to 49.5** after **trailing on the first count**, so it rewarded the broadly acceptable candidate over the biggest minority.

cards.front: Which electoral system gives seats equal to vote share, usually with a threshold?
cards.back: **Proportional representation (PR)**.

cards.front: What are the strengths and weaknesses of **PR**?
cards.back: **Strengths:** few wasted votes, **higher turnout**, far **more women and minorities** (lists and quotas). **Weaknesses:** no identifiable individual representative, **coalition instability**, small extremist parties gain outsized leverage.

cards.front: Contrast **closed list** and **open list** PR: who sets the candidate order?
cards.back: 1) **Closed list:** the **party** fixes the order → more party control, discipline, and easy quotas (Israel). 2) **Open list:** voters pick a **specific candidate** whose own votes decide → more voter choice but weaker, personalist parties (Brazil).
cards.hint: Party sets the rank vs voters set the rank.

cards.front: Which electoral family gives two ballots, a district candidate plus a party list?
cards.back: **Mixed / semiproportional** systems.

cards.front: Contrast Germany's **compensatory** and Japan's **noncompensatory** mixed systems.
cards.back: Both give a district vote plus a list vote. 1) **Compensatory (Germany):** the list tier tops seats up to full proportionality → highly proportional, multiparty. 2) **Noncompensatory (Japan):** the tiers stay **separate** → less proportional, more majoritarian.
cards.hint: Top up to proportional vs keep the tiers separate.

cards.front: What did Germany's **2023 electoral reform** change?
cards.back: It **capped the Bundestag at 630** and **scrapped overhang and compensatory seats**. Seats now follow the **list vote**, and a district win no longer guarantees a seat (*Zweitstimmendeckung*), so many now call it **"personalised PR"** rather than truly mixed.
cards.hint: Capped at 630; seats follow the list vote.

cards.front: Which law says SMD produces two parties and PR produces multiparty systems?
cards.back: **Duverger's Law**.

cards.front: By what two mechanisms does **SMD** push toward two parties (Duverger)?
cards.back: 1) **Mechanical effect:** small parties win **no seats** and wither. 2) **Psychological effect:** voters stop **wasting** votes on no hopers and defect to viable ones. Under PR both pressures vanish → multiparty survives.
cards.hint: Mechanical (no seats) plus psychological (no wasted votes).

cards.front: India runs a national multiparty system under FPTP, and France's two bloc system collapsed in 2017. What do these show about Duverger's Law?
cards.back: It is **not deterministic**; it holds in **established** democracies, not new or diverse ones. 1) **India:** diversity plus federalism plus non strategic identity voting (Moser & Scheiner). 2) **France 2017:** Macron's one year old party broke a near two party system.

cards.front: Name the five functions parties perform (FK deck).
cards.back: 1) **Mobilise** citizens. 2) **Recruit** the political elite. 3) **Simplify** choices. 4) **Organise government**. 5) **Provide opposition**.

cards.front: What single feature distinguishes parties from interest groups?
cards.back: **Parties seek office**; interest groups only seek influence.

cards.front: Which party system type: many parties compete freely but one wins every election? Give a case.
cards.back: **Dominant party** system. Case: the **ANC** in South Africa (won all six elections after apartheid; share fell to 57.5% in 2019).

cards.front: Which party system type has only two parties that can realistically win? Give a case.
cards.back: **Two party** system. Case: the **US** (no significant third party since the 1850s) and the UK.

cards.front: Which party system type has more than two parties that can win, forcing coalitions? Give a case.
cards.back: **Multiparty** system. Case: **Italy**.

cards.front: What is the thin line between a **dominant party** system and **electoral authoritarianism**?
cards.back: The test is **how** the party keeps winning: genuine **popularity** (still democratic) versus **rigging the rules, using state resources, and intimidating rivals** (authoritarian).

cards.front: Contrast the **sociological** and **institutional** explanations of party system size.
cards.back: 1) **Sociological:** parties grow from social **cleavages**, so the number of parties mirrors the number of deep divisions. 2) **Institutional (Duverger):** the **electoral rules** shape the count (SMD → two, PR → many).

cards.front: Which two classic 19th century cleavages shaped European party systems?
cards.back: 1) **Economic (capital versus labour)**: universal with industrialisation. 2) **Religious**: present in some countries only (Germany's CDU/CSU, but not all Catholic France).

cards.front: Match the mobilisation type: a party wins by offering ideas, ideology, and policy.
cards.back: **Programmatic** mobilisation. It thrives in established, richer democracies.

cards.front: Match the mobilisation type: a party trades material benefits for votes through local brokers.
cards.back: **Patronage / clientelist** mobilisation. It thrives in poorer, newer, statist economies.

cards.front: Match the mobilisation type: a personalist leader frames "the people" against a "corrupt elite".
cards.back: **Populist** mobilisation. It thrives anywhere in a "crisis of party democracy".

cards.front: Who argued voters mostly vote by social identity, not by weighing policy (the "folk theory" critique)?
cards.back: **Achen & Bartels**. So pure programmatic appeal is partly a myth.

cards.front: What are the two ideology axes parties map onto (FK / Von Beyme)?
cards.back: 1) **Horizontal: economic Left and Right** (redistribution). 2) **Vertical: cultural GAL TAN**. A party's position is the pair of coordinates.

cards.front: What do **GAL** and **TAN** stand for?
cards.back: **GAL** = Green/Alternative/Libertarian (progressive, cosmopolitan). **TAN** = Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist.

cards.front: On which axis and end does today's populist far right mainly mobilise?
cards.back: On the cultural axis, the **TAN** end (Farage, Salvini, AfD, RN, Fidesz).
cards.hint: The TAN end of the second axis.

cards.front: Diagnose the "crisis of party democracy": its symptoms and two competing explanations.
cards.back: **Symptoms:** only ~20% trust parties (though ~80% value democracy); falling loyalty, membership, and turnout; rising **volatility**; anti system parties. **Explanations:** **dealignment** (detach from all parties) versus **realignment** (switch allegiance); catch all parties becoming **"cartel parties" (Mair)** that collude at the centre.
cards.hint: Low trust · dealign vs realign · cartel parties.

cards.front: Contrast **dealignment** and **realignment**.
cards.back: 1) **Dealignment:** voters **detach from all parties**. 2) **Realignment:** voters **switch** their allegiance to different parties.

cards.front: Who coined "cartel parties" for catch all parties colluding at the centre?
cards.back: **Mair**.

cards.front: What does **The PopuList** (Rooduijn et al. 2024) show about anti establishment voting in Europe?
cards.back: Across 31 countries the combined anti establishment vote **roughly doubled**, from ~12% (1993) to ~31% (2022), driven mainly by **far right populists**.

cards.front: Why is the **US** a partial exception to the dealignment story?
cards.back: Not dealignment but partisan **sorting and polarisation (Abramowitz)**, racial realignment, and Trump's **status threat** populism (**Mutz 2018**).
cards.hint: Sorting and status threat, not detachment.

cards.front: Contrast **pluralism** and **neocorporatism** as interest group models.
cards.back: 1) **Pluralism (US):** **many** competing groups around a **neutral** state; easy entry but fragmented clout. 2) **Neocorporatism (Germany, N. Europe):** a **few** hierarchical **peak associations** negotiate **binding** deals; more influence but less participatory.
cards.hint: Many and loose vs few and binding.

cards.front: Who said the pluralist heaven's chorus "sings with a strong upper class accent"?
cards.back: **Schattschneider**: who gets organised is skewed toward the well off.

cards.front: Who argued that in pluralism **business is inherently privileged**?
cards.back: **Lindblom**.

cards.front: What is a **peak association**?
cards.back: A body uniting a whole sector to negotiate with the state (peak labour, peak industry, peak employers).

cards.front: What is **state corporatism**?
cards.back: The mandated, authoritarian version of corporatism, imposed by the state rather than voluntary.

cards.front: What is **social capital**?
cards.back: Networks plus norms of reciprocity that underpin civil society.

cards.front: Match the position on civil society: civic **decline**.
cards.back: **Putnam**, in *Bowling Alone*.

cards.front: Match the position: mass membership bodies gave way to **managed advocacy**.
cards.back: **Skocpol**.

cards.front: Match the position: civic activity has just **moved to new forms**.
cards.back: **Dalton**, in "Kicking in Groups" (movements, single issue groups).

cards.front: State the **Powell trade off**.
cards.back: **Diverse representation and participation** versus **clear accountability and governability**. Every design chooses a point on this line; there is no free lunch.

cards.front: Which designs sit at each end of the Powell trade off?
cards.back: 1) **Open to diversity (PR, multiparty, pluralism):** maximise representation but blur accountability. 2) **Majoritarian (first past the post, two party):** clear accountability but wasted votes and worse representation of minorities.

cards.front: What is the chapter's most robust empirical finding about PR and women?
cards.back: **PR represents women far better than SMD** (Nordic 42.5% versus US House 23.4%; India adds reserved seats).

cards.front: How does **Iversen & Soskice** link the electoral system to redistribution?
cards.back: 1) **PR:** the middle class allies with the poor → **bigger** welfare states. 2) **Majoritarian:** the middle allies with the rich → **smaller** welfare states. So electoral systems shape policy, not just seats.
cards.hint: PR → middle plus poor → bigger welfare.

cards.front: What is the empirical tell from Iversen & Soskice (1945 to 1998)?
cards.back: Counting years of left versus right government: under **PR the right governed only 26%** of the time; under **majoritarian, 75%**. Same democracies, opposite tilt.

cards.front: Which case: UKIP won 12.6% of the vote but only 1 seat, while the SNP won fewer votes yet 56 seats?
cards.back: **UK** (SMD / first past the post, two party): extreme **disproportionality** and wasted votes.

cards.front: Which case: the whole country is one district with a 3.25% threshold and held three elections in 2019?
cards.back: **Israel** (pure closed list PR): hyper multiparty **instability** under extreme diversity.

cards.front: Which case: open list PR with no threshold produced 30 parties by 2018?
cards.back: **Brazil**: weak party **fragmentation** plus populism (Rousseff impeached 2016, Bolsonaro won 2018).

cards.front: Which case: FPTP plus federalism, with 120 of ~600 seats reserved for lower castes and tribes?
cards.back: **India**: Duverger's limits in a diverse democracy plus reserved seat representation (BJP 2014: 31% of vote → 52% of seats).

cards.front: Germany and Japan both run mixed systems, yet Germany is multiparty and Japan was LDP dominated. Explain.
cards.back: 1) **Germany:** compensatory PR plus a 5% threshold tops seats to proportionality → stable multiparty (Greens 1983, AfD 2017). 2) **Japan:** noncompensatory (1994 reform, tiers kept separate) → more majoritarian; the **LDP dominated 1955 to 1993**.
cards.hint: Compensatory top up vs separate tiers.

cards.front: What four questions should you run for any electoral system case?
cards.back: 1) Which system? 2) How do votes become seats? 3) How many parties result (Duverger)? 4) Who gets left out, and what is traded off (representation versus accountability)?
cards.hint: System → votes to seats → party count → who is left out.

cards.front: Tie the lecture together: the chain from participation to representation and the two spine questions.
cards.back: **Chain:** electoral system → party system → interest group system decides whose interests get represented, and the **electoral system is the master lever**. **Spine questions:** 1) Why participate (a collective action problem institutions shape)? 2) Whose interests get represented (the chain)? Underneath sits the **Powell trade off**, and it all starts from **Pitkin's** question of what representation means.
cards.hint: Electoral → party → interest group; why participate plus who is represented.
